To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the noise-power-ratio method produces optimistic small-singular in-band distortion measurements for microwave power amplifiers, that this effect is independent of the notch width, and that a harmonic-balance simulator can be used as an alternative means to evaluate the corrected co-channel distortion-ratio.
the conventional noise-power-ratios produce optimistic small-signal distortion measurements when compared to continuous-spectrum excitation and that this effect increases with the notch width.

the co-channel distortion ratio is a function of the input signal spectrum and that the conventional noise-power-ratios test is optimistic when compared to a continuous spectrum excitation, as the notch width decreases.

, in the presence of a notch in the spectrum, a conventional noise power ratio test overestimates the distortion ratio, while a co-channel power ratio test provides a more realistic value.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the conventional co-channel noise-power-ratio measurement method produces optimistic results when compared to a theoretical continuous spectrum excitation method.

a co-channel distortion ratio measurement, based on a conventional power ratio test, can be used as a small-signal inband distortion measurement, provided that the amplifier is memoryless mildly nonlinear and the notch width is small.
the conventional noise-power-ratios test produces optimistic small signal distortion measurements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the co-channel distortion ratio can be accurately evaluated using a novel setup, and that it can be predicted using the harmonic-balance method.

a conventional noise power ratio (NPR) measurement is not an accurate indicator of the in-band distortion performance of a power amplifier, when the amplifier is operating at large back-off from its saturation power.
a corrected co-channel power ratio is a better indicator of the in-band distortion than a conventional noise-power ratio, especially for a saturated power amplifier.
